prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform large-volume lumbar puncture before MRI excludes mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Do not infer iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone — DESH, callosal angle <90°, and a clinical triad are required
Do not diagnose Alzheimer's disease in a patient with gait-predominant presentation and ventriculomegaly without first excluding NPH
Do not attribute the syndrome to 'normal ageing' or 'deconditioning' once the imaging criteria for ventriculomegaly are met
required_recommendations: Obtain brain MRI before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Document objective pre-tap gait (TUG and 10-metre walk) and a brief cognitive baseline so that pre/post-tap change can be quantified
Remove 30-50 mL of CSF during the tap test (a low-volume LP under-samples and biases the test toward false negative)
Re-assess gait and cognition 1-4 hours after the tap and again at 24 hours (the response window for tap-test prediction of shunt benefit)
Refer to neurosurgery for VP shunt evaluation when imaging, clinical, and tap-test criteria support iNPH

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific for NPH and does not distinguish from neurodegenerative alternatives in this chronic gait/cognitive presentation
ECG is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of chronic gait + cognitive + urinary triad once cardiogenic syncope is not on the differential
Echocardiography does not contribute to NPH evaluation in the absence of syncope or cardioembolic stroke workup
Head CT is inferior to MRI for measuring Evans index and callosal angle and for excluding secondary causes; only justified if MRI is contraindicated
Cardiac monitoring has no diagnostic role in NPH and is reserved for syncope or arrhythmia workup

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Small-vessel disease can produce gait apraxia and executive slowing, but ventriculomegaly out of proportion to white-matter burden and a positive tap test favour NPH
Shuffling gait overlaps, but absence of resting tremor, asymmetric rigidity, or L-dopa response and presence of magnetic gait + DESH favour NPH

Cognitive decline overlaps; AD typically presents with episodic-memory predominance and hippocampal atrophy rather than frontal-subcortical pattern and magnetic gait; targeted CSF Alzheimer biomarkers can evaluate suspected copathology when the result would change counselling or management

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventriculomegaly proportionate to sulcal widening, callosal angle >90°, and absence of DESH or transependymal signal argue against true NPH
No history of trauma, SAH, or meningitis on review; would be considered if history suggested antecedent intracranial event

key_clinical_evidence: iNPH diagnosis (Relkin 2005 INPH Study Group) requires (a) Hakim's triad of gait disturbance, cognitive impairment, and urinary urgency/incontinence — gait is typically first and most prominent; (b) ventriculomegaly with Evans >0.3 and DESH on MRI without mass effect; (c) age >40 and chronic course; (d) opening pressure <25 cmH2O; (e) absence of an alternative explanation
MRI is the imaging modality of choice — measure Evans index and callosal angle (<90° supports NPH) and confirm DESH (tight high-convexity sulci + wide Sylvian fissures)

The tap test removes 30-50 mL of CSF after measuring opening pressure and compares prespecified objective gait and cognitive measures before and after drainage; a positive response supports shunt responsiveness, while a negative single tap does not exclude NPH
Tap-test sensitivity is only 50-80%; a single negative tap does not exclude NPH — an extended (3-5 day) lumbar drainage trial can resolve borderline cases

Reversible-cause laboratory tests do not diagnose NPH and are optional; order targeted tests only when the presentation suggests a metabolic, endocrine, infectious, inflammatory, vitamin, or medication-related mimic
Alzheimer copathology is common in iNPH and may reduce cognitive benefit from shunting without necessarily eliminating gait benefit
Shunt response is best predicted by an objectively positive tap test or extended drainage trial in a patient who meets imaging and clinical criteria
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: The reversible-cause screen is good practice but does not establish or exclude hydrocephalus; the tap test does.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede large-volume LP to exclude mass effect or secondary obstructive hydrocephalus before removing 30-50 mL of CSF
The baseline gait and cognition must be measured before the large-volume tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted and the tap test yields nothing

patient.history_present_illness: A 71-year-old right-handed retired nurse with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and history of left knee replacement was admitted from the neurology outpatient clinic for inpatient tap trial evaluation after 14 months of progressive triad symptoms. The patient, a former nurse who is knowledgeable about her own health, first noticed gait changes approximately 14 months ago — she describes her feet as feeling 'like they are stuck to the floor' and she began using a walker after two near-falls in the home. She notes that her gait instability is disproportionate to the bilateral knee pain — she has had worsening bilateral knee osteoarthritis but her orthopedic surgeon told her that her gait pattern is 'not just the arthritis.' Over approximately the same period she has developed urinary urgency that occasionally results in urge incontinence before reaching the bathroom. She wears pads 'just in case.' Her daughter has noted she is more 'vague' and 'slow to respond' in conversations over the past 8 months — she repeats herself more and takes longer to find words than previously. She scored 21/30 on MoCA at the outpatient appointment (loses on attention, trail-making, and recall). Brain MRI obtained outpatient showed 'communicating hydrocephalus with moderate white matter disease.' Evans index measured at 0.32 on outpatient review. Callosal angle was measured at 96 degrees on coronal imaging — equivocal (borderline value is <90 degrees for NPH). Admission is for high-volume tap trial.
